Date: 2025-09-11
Start: 16:30 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Jamal Ortiz (Cobalt - Platform), Li Wei (Cobalt - Security), Sara Thompson (Cobalt - ML)
Notes: technical deep dive focused on where to place safety/moderation filters in the inference stack (pre-gen, in-model, post-gen async), performance overhead, and deployment constraints for VPC/on-prem.
summary: SE-led deep dive exploring tradeoffs of moderation placement. Discussed synchronous gateway filters vs in-pipeline token-level blocking vs async post-processing. Evaluated cost and tail-latency impact, KV cache and batching interactions, and on-prem constraints (no external egress). Agreed on benchmark plan: run pre-filter proxy on CPU, lightweight GPU classifier baseline, and dedicated GPU pipeline for heavy classifiers. Next: Redwood to run microbenchmarks with customer's trace; customer to provide sample prompts.
topics: moderation placement options (pre / in-model / post async)
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining on the deep dive. can you hear me ok?
[00:03] Jamal Ortiz: yes loud and clear, thanks alex.
[00:07] Priya Nair: hi all, priya here, i'll drive the tech bit and we can jump into where you currently run filters and what your constraints are.
[00:14] Li Wei: perfect. quick context — Cobalt needs zero-external-egress for PHI-related prompts, and security wants tamper-proof audit logs, plus SOC2 type2 is a must.
[00:25] Sara Thompson: and for product, the latency SLO is 300ms p95 for the interactive assistant. throughput peaks around 120 reqs/s for the busiest endpoints.
[00:34] Priya Nair: good — that's tight. so the core decision is placement of the safety/moderation step: pre-filter at the API gateway (cheap CPU classifier), in-model heuristics (token-level blocking), or post-gen async checks that can redact or trigger fallback. each has pros/cons.
[00:50] Jamal Ortiz: can you walk perf numbers at a high level? like how much does a synchronous pre-filter add vs in-pipeline?
[00:56] Priya Nair: sure. ballpark from our internal benches: a lightweight CPU-based classifier (binary safety) is ~20-50ms median on a 4-core server, p95 maybe 80-120ms under load. a heavier transformer-based filter on GPU is ~60-120ms depending on model and batch size. token-level in-model checks are effectively zero-add per request for the generation step but they increase complexity: they impact KV cache and can reduce batching efficiency because you may need shorter sequences or synchronous decisions mid-stream.
[01:23] Li Wei: mid-stream decisions — that's the token-level approach? we worry about partial hallucinations and safety needing token-level intervention.
[01:29] Priya Nair: yeah, token-level is the most precise: you can block unsafe tokens as they are generated, but it's intrusive. you need an integrated safety head or close coupling with the runtime. it complicates caching: the KV cache can no longer be treated purely as stateless prefix cache because state depends on the filter decisions. that can reduce KV hit rates by 10-30% in some workloads we saw.
[01:47] Sara Thompson: so that would worsen latency overall?
[01:50] Priya Nair: it tends to increase tail latency and reduce throughput — smaller batches and more frequent flushes. So tradeoff: better control vs economics.
[01:57] Alex Chen: another option is do a pre-filter for obvious stuff and escalate borderline cases to an async heavy pipeline that runs in parallel. if the heavy path flags something post-gen you can redact or follow up with a mitigation flow.
[02:10] Jamal Ortiz: but if we redact post-hoc, product gets weird UX — user saw something then it disappears. not ideal for support workloads.
[02:17] Priya Nair: agreed, UX tradeoff. For support tickets we often recommend synchronous decision for safety-critical categories and async for lower-risk categories. mixing patterns is common: pre-filter on CPU for high recall but low precision, then for matches you either block immediately or route to a dedicated GPU safety pipeline for higher-precision classification.
[02:36] Li Wei: how does batching interact with that routing? if we route to GPU safety pipeline doesn't that break batching on the main generator because it's waiting for a safety verdict?
[02:43] Priya Nair: it can. best pattern: do the cheap pre-filter synchronously and let the generator proceed. For matches flagged as "needs review", you either: 1) stall generation while you run deep classifier (bad for latency), 2) optimistically stream content with a visible watermark and run async review (bad UX), or 3) run a lightweight fast classifier on CPU to reduce escalations to GPU. The default we suggest for interactive apps is (3).
[03:06] Sara Thompson: any numbers on cost deltas? we need to justify dedicated GPU pool for safety.
[03:11] Alex Chen: rough numbers: CPU pre-filter cost is low — a handful of cents per thousand requests — GPU classifier for heavy models can add tens to hundreds of dollars per million requests depending on runtime and batching. Dedicated pooled GPUs for safety help amortize per-request cost if you have high sustained volume.
[03:26] Priya Nair: important nuance: batching for classifiers can reduce per-request cost but increases latency. For example, a GPU classifier batched at 64 can have great throughput (low cost per item) but p95 latency goes up — sometimes to 200-400ms depending on GPU and sequence length. If your p95 budget is 300ms for the whole pipeline, a 200-400ms classifier eats too much headroom.
[03:47] Jamal Ortiz: you mentioned KV cache earlier — can pre-filtering improve or hurt KV cache hit rates?
[03:52] Priya Nair: pre-filtering generally helps KV cache because you can normalize inputs before they hit the model — strip emojis, canonicalize prompts — leading to higher cache hits. But token-level modifications (like in-model edits) create divergent state and lower shared cache reuse. Also batching patterns: if pre-filtering introduces variability in request size or causes per-request branching, it can reduce batch sizes, so cache and batching are linked.
transcript_continued:
[04:20] Sara Thompson: what about quantization — if we quantize the safety model to int8, what's the impact on precision?
[04:26] Priya Nair: quantization often keeps inference accuracy high for classification tasks, int8 usually within a few percent of fp16 for many safety classifiers, but you must validate on your prompt sets. The upside is reduced memory and faster throughput which can make on-prem deployment viable on cheaper GPUs or even CPU-friendly runtimes.
[04:43] Li Wei: for on-prem, we cannot call external moderation APIs. so options are to ship a local filter model or run the filter in isolated VPC. any caveats?
[04:52] Priya Nair: on-prem means you need local model binaries and a local runtime. That increases operational surface: model updates, patching, and monitoring are now on you. If you use Redwood Private, we support private model bundles and locked-down control plane. Network egress: if the heavy classifier needs external threat intel, that's blocked in air-gapped setups; you either include that data offline or accept reduced coverage. Also KMS/HSM integration for keys is supported but requires provisioning.
[05:17] Alex Chen: one architecture we've seen: run the main generator on Redwood Dedicated GPUs, run a lightweight CPU pre-filter in the VPC, escalate to a dedicated on-prem GPU pool for heavy classification. That keeps egress zero and gives you predictable cost via reserved capacity.
[05:32] Jamal Ortiz: how do we measure the real-world impact? can Redwood run tests against our traces?
[05:36] Alex Chen: yes — that's part of the next steps. Priya will produce a benchmark plan and we'll run three configs: (A) CPU pre-filter only, (B) CPU pre-filter + GPU heavy classifier sync, (C) CPU pre-filter + async GPU review and optimistic stream. We'll report p50/p95/p99 latencies, KV hit rates, batching efficiency, and cost per 1M requests.
[05:56] Sara Thompson: please include sample prompts that are domain-specific — PHI redaction is tricky.
[06:00] Priya Nair: absolutely. Jamal, if you can share anonymized traces and three canonical prompt sets we'll include those as the basis for the bench.
[06:07] Jamal Ortiz: will do.
[06:10] Li Wei: curious on SDK and observability — we need token-level audit trails if we do token-level blocking. can you provide that?
[06:17] Priya Nair: Redwood Console captures per-request traces, token counts, model versions, and we can enable enhanced audit logs showing decisions from the safety pipeline as structured events. For on-prem we'll ship the same hooks but retention may be configured by you.
[06:30] Alex Chen: quick interruption — competitor question: do you use Anthropic's safety APIs in any reference archs?
[06:35] Priya Nair: we evaluate competitor models but we don't route customer data to third-party moderation by default without explicit configuration. you can choose to run third-party models with explicit consent.
[06:44] Sara Thompson: operational question — can we do canary rollouts for a new safety model? we want to start at 1% of traffic.
[06:50] Priya Nair: yes — Redwood supports traffic routing by rules. you can start a canary that routes 1% of requests for a route to a new safety pipeline and monitor false positive/negative rates. If it looks bad we can rollback automatically.
[06:59] Jamal Ortiz: what about fallback policies — if the safety pipeline times out should generator fall back to a safer default or block?
[07:05] Priya Nair: you define policies. common defaults: on timeout, either block the generation and return a safety error, or fallback to a smaller/safer model and reduce output length. There is also a graceful degrade option: return a short apology + escalate to support. We'll include policy templates in the docs.
[07:20] Sara Thompson: any gotchas with SSO and KMS for Private? we use an HSM internally.
[07:25] Alex Chen: we support SAML SSO and integrate with customer KMS/HSM for key wrapping and audit proof. For on-prem, keys are customer-managed and we can validate via mutual TLS.
[07:36] Li Wei: curious about throughput math — can we get a sample calc for cost/throughput with batching and KV cache hit rate?
[07:43] Priya Nair: yes — example: assume 120 req/s, avg token output 60 tokens, KV cache hit 40%. With batching you can average batch sizes of 8-16 depending on concurrency; token-level compute reduces when cache hits increase. We'll run the calc with your traces.
[07:58] Jamal Ortiz: I worry about the number of false positives from a cheap CPU filter; too many flags will send traffic to gpu pipeline and spike costs.
[08:04] Priya Nair: exactly — that's why tuning and a multi-stage approach works: pick a high-recall CPU model and then a precision-focused GPU model for escalations. Also consider a small ensemble where you run a fast heuristic first, then a tiny transformer on CPU for triage instead of always escalating to GPU.
[08:22] Sara Thompson: what's the instrumentation cost for tracking decisions? is that a lot of telemetry?
[08:26] Priya Nair: it's metadata — decision codes, model id, confidence — small per-request overhead. Storage cost depends on retention window. Redwood Console can ingest these events; if you want full token-level transcripts for every request storage will grow quickly, so we usually recommend selective retention for flagged events.
[08:44] Alex Chen: switching to deployment specifics: for air-gapped customers we do image bundles plus a private control plane that runs in your VPC. updates are via signed artifacts. Any concerns from ops?
[08:55] Jamal Ortiz: patching cadence and regression testing — we need guarantees on rollback.
[08:59] Priya Nair: we provide rollback tooling and can run canary model rollouts within your VPC. we also ship a validation harness to run your prompt set before promoting a new model.
[09:10] Li Wei: is there a recommended sequence to reduce initial risk? like start with pre-filter, then add in-model signals?
[09:16] Priya Nair: recommended phased approach: 1) baseline: deploy a CPU pre-filter + observability, 2) monitor and tune thresholds, 3) add precision GPU pipeline for escalations, run it in parallel as log-only initially, 4) enable sync escalations for critical categories, 5) evaluate token-level integration if you need per-token blocking. That reduces user impact and gives measurable ROI at each stage.
[09:40] Sara Thompson: can you show sample configs for the pre-filter to make it deterministic and stable?
[09:44] Priya Nair: yes — we'll share the sample config: threshold levels, categories to block vs escalate, and normalization rules. We'll include examples in the benchmark repo.
[09:53] Alex Chen: Ok let's quick recap before we run out of time. Priya — deliver bench plan. Alex — send security docs and pricing. Jamal — share traces + prompts. Li Wei — confirm SOC2 questions list. Anyone else?
[10:05] Li Wei: I'll follow up with a short list of compliance questions.
[10:08] Sara Thompson: thanks everyone.
[10:10] Alex Chen: thanks all, we'll target next sync after we share the bench results.
[10:13] Jamal Ortiz: thanks. bye.
